utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. Yesterday, I asked the parties to update the Chamber about the disclosure of material for the Defence counsel in another case. Is it possible to update the Chamber now? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have reviewed the order, reviewed our material and found there's nothing that was the subject of the order that we have any problem with the Popovic people receiving. In fact, we continue ongoing discovery in this case with all the Popovic folks, as we always have in the trial, so discovery-wise nothing has really changed and as I recall the order did not apply to ex parte filings. So, basically, we're an open book to the Popovic case. There's nothing that we need pulled back or not provided them in this case, from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't fully understand the position. In our decision, we were talking about confidential material related to personal information about our accused, Mr. Tolimir, and possible family members. They were excluded by our decision from the disclosure. Is -- all material of our case, Tolimir case, disclosed to the Defence counsel in the other case? Or what is the -- the situation at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All the substantive witness statements, collections, all the material that we send out to General Tolimir, we, at the same time, send out and have been sending out to the Popovic team. That doesn't always include filings and sometimes people want filings, but we have no objection to Registry providing any filings in this case or any -- anything like that. We have no problem with any of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Gajic, what is your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, everyone. Mr. President as for the Defence, we have nothing against any document or submission submitted by the Defence be provided to the parties in the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this update. The witness should be brought in, please. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just a translation update, Mr. President. We now have translations for Exhibit P01362. So that -- that's been solved. And you asked me, I believe it was yesterday, to see if there were any issues related to translation and Mr. Brunborg exhibits, and we have been discussing about that with Mr. Gajic, and we don't -- we don't have any issues. There's nothing that is outstanding for that. And Mr. Gajic has gotten back to us about -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please sit down, Mr. Brunborg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He has gotten back to us on Mr. Hagland's voluminous exhibits and has picked out a few things that he would like us to translate which shouldn't be a problem, an article or two. There's one 20-page book that we're struggling with CLSS to get translated, but I think we'll find a way to do it and so that shouldn't be a problem either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: When will we receive the final information if all the requested translation have been made in order to admit these documents into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can't really say, Mr. President. CLSS is -- is -- and -- is difficult to predict. I would say, hopefully within 30 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon, Mr. Brunborg.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome back to the courtroom. The -- I shall remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And Mr. Tolimir is continuing his cross-examination. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, before we continue, sir, I was asked yesterday about -- by Mr. McCloskey about duplicates in the missing list identified by the Defence expert Radovanovic in the Blagojevic case and I said I did not quite remember, and I looked at our previous reports and I would like just to clarify that question, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That would be very helpful for the Chamber and the parties. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Mrs. Radovanovic, using the same data as we used, identified five certain and five unlike examples of highly likely duplicates. Those five -- most misused the term certain duplicates where had also been identified by us and marked as such, but as I said, we had, through an oversight, not removed them. Of the five additional likely duplicates found by -- identified by Mrs. Radovanovic, three were identified by all us, quite likely duplicates, two were found not to be duplicates. So out of her ten, eight were duplicates and five had previously been identified by us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May I wish for peace in this house and may the proceedings here today end according to God's will and not according to mine. I would like to welcome the witness back and to wish a good afternoon to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, we stopped at a question which was unanswered, and the question was: Whether you and Mr. Dusan Janc and Mr. Dean Manning worked together in the Prosecutor's office of this Tribunal? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. No, I never worked together with these gentlemen. Dean Manning was working here for part of the time I was here, and I talked to him, but we never -- now and then -- but not on the subject matters in any detail. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at 65 ter 1708 that we called up yesterday towards the end of the day. This is 65 ter 1708. This is a paper, an article, authored by you, sir. It's called "The accounting for genocide: How many were killed in Srebrenica?" And while we're waiting for the document to appear -- actually, we can already see it. I'm going to put my question. On page 3 of this article of yours - can we look at page 3, please - and the last issue is what is the number of victims that has to be established, what is the number of victims that has to be established in order for someone to be tried for genocide? Have you found the place? It's paragraph 3, the last sentence. In the course of your work for the Tribunal, did you receive any kind of interpretation from your co-workers, investigators, that you needed to establish a certain number of victims in order to be able to convict someone of genocide? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. No, I never received any information or instruction on that. But what I learned was that I was referred to the Statute of the ICTY, which is quoted in the immediate sentence that, according to the ICTY Statute, genocide is defined as acts committed with intent to destroy in whole or in part a national ethnic or religious group. So according to this -- this definition, it is -- there's no number, no proportion. In fact, according to this, a person could be convicted for genocide without killing anybody, since the intent here is crucial. So I did not receive -- nobody has established that there is a certain number of victims or -- or certain proportion of population that's -- that has to be exterminated for the genocide to apply in a legal setting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you then, in your report, describe how many inhabitants from Srebrenica were transferred to Tuzla in July 1995 by the Army of Republika Srpska through its territory?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that -- no, that was not part of the mandate I was given. We looked only at missing and dead persons in connection with the fall of Srebrenica, not on displaced persons or refugees. So I -- I've seen estimates of the flow but uncertain estimates. I don't know if such precise estimates exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to clarify, we know he has got reports in this case and this document up on the screen may be considered a report as well, so for the record could we just make -- I think I know what his answer referred to but I'm not sure which report the General's question referred to, and it may not be clear. If we can just clear that up before -- before it gets passed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it is clear that, at the moment, Mr. Tolimir is dealing with this report we have on the screen. This is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. But his answer was the mandate that he had for the Prosecution. I think it was for the report that he is talking about. That is what is completely unclear in my view, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then I would like that ask you, Mr. Brunborg. Your mandate, did that have anything to do with this article you wrote?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at all. This -- this article was written after I left the Tribunal. It was written on my own or the time of Statistics Norway as an academic article, based on my experience and previous reports but not at all part of the mandate given to me by OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, that was the report that I was thinking of. Can we now look at page 4 of the document that we have in front of you in order to answer Mr. McCloskey's question. Can we look at page 4 in the Serbian. It's also page 4 in the English. I'm looking at the second paragraph which states: "The research questions that guided the demographic projects on Srebrenica were defined by the Office of the Prosecutor as ..." I quote what you wrote: "What was the minimum number of victims from Srebrenica who were killed by the VRS after the fall of the enclave on the 11th of July 1995 who can be identified by name? And how is that list of victims reliable?"

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So can you please explain how you went about the task that was formulated for you in this way by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. First, I would like to say that the first bullet point: What was number of victims from Srebrenica who were killed by the VRS? Well, the OTP did not, as far as I remember, include that specifically in the requests for data and analysis. They were just asking to -- for the minimum number of victims. But I knew, of course, in the conversations and the contact with OTP and other reading that there had a been -- there was an armed conflict and that the VRS -- the public -- the Army of Republika Srpska attacked Srebrenica and -- and it fell. So, but, who -- who was killed was not part of my mandate. It was the missing and dead. Sorry, who killed these persons was not part of the mandate. And how I went about it was to collect data on missing and dead persons from the ICRC, PHR, and other possible sources, and to evaluate, assess, compare these lists as we talked at length about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And if that is the way you just told us, can you please tell us why you are presenting this -- in this particular way to the academic community? Because you are quoting or you are stating what I quoted back to you, that you, as an investigator, or a researcher, had received the research questions that guided the demographic project on Srebrenica. So they were defined by the Office of the Prosecutor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I must admit, I don't remember the exact wording of the requests which came orally not in writing, I think. And whether it was exactly this wording, I don't remember. This is now, what, 12 years ago. So it is possible here if the killing thing is an issue that we introduced these terms as to help the academic reader. After all, it had been established in the Krstic trial that there had been executions by the VRS of missing persons -- or, of persons from Srebrenica. But, again - sorry - my point is that who killed these people was not part of my mandate. It was only to find out how many and their names and other particulars.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, in which way you established who killed them? What was the research procedure that you, as a demographer, used to establish whether somebody was killed in combat or perhaps in some kind of mutual conflict?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said repeatedly, I did not establish, and my colleagues and I did not establish, how people were killed in combat or not, and who killed them. We were only asked to find the number of missing and possibly dead persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If that is so, then can you please tell me if you were informed at all by the OTP about these events. Nobody gave you anything. You were just told to do the research but were you informed at all about what happened, because according to you, sometimes this happened and sometimes that happened, and now it turns out that nobody gave you anything. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I was told what happened. I think on the very first day at the OTP, I asked why did the events in Srebrenica happen so late in the conflict? And I was then given -- I asked one senior lawyer and I was then given a book to read -- David Rohde, a book on Srebrenica, and I read other books and I saw the B/C/S Panorama movie about Srebrenica which I think was provided by the OTP. So, of course, I wanted to know and I learned about the events in Srebrenica. Actually, before I was tasked to estimate the number of dead and missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Do you have the full title of the book that you were given to read? The author and the title.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The author is David Rohde, R-o-h-d-e, and I can find the -- and I think it is -- the full title is given in the reference lists of the article that we are just discussing. I will look it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you said R-o-h-d-e.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: R-o-h-d -- sorry, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But it was recorded in a different way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, right now I don't quite remember. No, it is not given there, but I'll check and find that reference later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It is a well-known book. I can give you the name of it, if you'd like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I would appreciate, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In England, it is called: "A Safe Area." And in the United States it is called: "The End Game."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: By David Rohde?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: David Rohde, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, now I remember the book I read was called "The End Game," very thick book, very well written, very interesting. But I also read other books and other articles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Brunborg, we are now looking at page 3 of your paper where you talk about the attempt to destroy the Muslim population after the capture of Srebrenica and that it represents the most serious and the most obvious example of genocide in the war in the former Yugoslavia. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are now seeing page 4, at least in the English version. Yes, I see --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If we can look at page 3. I don't know if you've found it. It's on page 3.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Which paragraph, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the text in English. I think it's the fourth paragraph. It's the second half of the fourth paragraph in English.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And your question is?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: You, as a demographer, have you studied the persecutions and massacres over Serbs which were committed in this same area by those very same Serbs that here you claim tried to actually annihilate the Muslims. So have you read any other books, books about annihilation of Serbs in Sarajevo, in Central Bosnia, in the Medak pocket in Croatia and elsewhere, if you are talking about the genocide over a population or a part thereof?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've regard articles, I'm not aware of any full book about massacres of Serbs elsewhere in Bosnia. I knew there were events where also there were Serb victims, but I studied the -- the -- the fall of Srebrenica and the massacre of the killings that happened there. The quotation is then -- well, it is -- the last sentence in the paragraph you are referring to referred to authors Honig and Booth, and, indeed, Rohde 1997. So that sentence is based on the reading of their books.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that those same Muslims, in Srebrenica, during less than one whole year, 1993, killed about three and a half thousands Serbs in this very same zone that are you write being here?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I've read about -- about attacks, killings, also of Serbs, but that was not part of my study. But I have read about it, and I know there were attacks on Serb village, et cetera. But, again, it was not part of my survey or study.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Shouldn't the subject of your analysis be what is the cause of all this; and did you research the fact that the greatest part of the population from that zone was let go? And how can it be called a genocide if women and children from the same population were let go? How can you call that a genocide? Could you explain us that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The genocide term was not given by me but by the Judges in the Krstic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But you informed the public about it. In your articles you defined it as a genocide. You are standing behind it as an author, as -- and as a public figure engaged in the research of this subject; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct and this article was written after the trial of Krstic so we could safely base our terminology on the findings of the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 2 of this same article -- can we have page 2 in e-court because I would like to ask a question about it and I would like the witness to see the page. I'm going to quote you. You said: "Accounting for genocide is not an exact science." You remember that. My question is: If it is not an exact science, then what kind of science is it then?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, genocide is -- sorry. Genocide is used in different ways. It is also used in the legal profession by courts which is the case here. But it is also -- genocide is also used by historians, economists, sociologists, anthropologists, in many -- in many disciplines. And there is no exact definition of genocide, except for the Statute of ICTY, and ICC, and similar courts. If I may add, usually in the sort of more popular terminology, genocide is used for large killings, when many people are killed. But according to the legal terminology, that is it not necessarily the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You haven't quite answered my question, because I asked you if it's not a science, how would you define it. But, all right, it's exactly irrelevant for the continuation of these proceedings. Since, in this article of yours, there is no mention whatsoever about the fact that this column which was trying to breakthrough from Srebrenica towards Tuzla, that it used the axis along which there were combat activities, and you are also not mentioning anything about the resistance given by the VRS. How can it be said then that you are writing a reliable demographic analysis? You are calling it here -- all right, I'm not going to quote it, but you call it some sort of science. Can it really be possible that it is a science then?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This article is about the number of people who were -- went missing or were killed in the fall of Srebrenica. And, as such, the events on the way to -- to Tuzla do not -- are not really that relevant. We mention that some -- many -- an unknown number of persons went through the forest to the free territory, but what happened on the way is not really part of our story.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit -- Defence number D159. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Have you analysed any Muslim documents in order to arrive to this conclusion that there had existed an intention to annihilate the Muslim population there?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I'm not aware of -- what you call the Muslim document. I don't know what you -- what you mean by a Muslim document. But we were mainly concerned with lists of missing and dead and different reports and articles. It's possible that some of what we read was written by Muslims, but I do not recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to read only one report by the commander of BiH army, Rasim Delic, that he wrote on the day of the breakthrough of this column. This is what he says: "The units of the 28th Division are moving out of Srebrenica while still fighting. The units of the 28th Division are still compact in the temporarily occupied territory. They are successful. They have inflicted huge casualties to the aggressor during the combat. So far, they have eight Chetniks that they have captured alive. The units of the 28th Division of land army managed to link up with the units of the 2nd Corps that had been infiltrated there. Jointly, they continue the fighting in the temporarily occupied territory." By that, they mean the territory of Republika Srpska: "Activities are being undertaken in order to profit from these activities." So, this is what General Delic wrote on 16th of July, 1995. That was exactly when those units were breaking out while fighting through the territory of Republika Srpska. So, he, as a commander, says that they managed to pull out, and you say that genocide was perpetrated on them. Aren't those two things contradictory, your thesis and his report? Or whatever it is that you are trying to say on a basis of some sort of science? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Dr. Brunborg has clearly said he based the genocide on the Krstic judgement, so the question is now being: Compare the Krstic judgement to Delic's report, and I just don't think that gets us anywhere. I mean, does he really want to open the Krstic judgement to be part of the litigation in this case, and does that open up the Popovic judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was wondering which purpose these questions have. On the other hand, it is the right of the accused to put questions to the witness in relation to the article he wrote. That has something to do with professionalism, his background, how he came to certain conclusions. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I absolutely agree with the Court on that, and that's why you haven't seen me get up. But his -- his question implied that the witness had made a personal assessment of the genocide, and the witness has denied that repeatedly and said he is just repeating Krstic. So he is misstating the evidence, he is misstating the testimony in his question. And that's just not allowed, because -- it doesn't take us any of where. The article is a potential -- is absolutely open -- open season on the article, no problem with that. But now he is going beyond it and suggesting something the witness specifically has rejected several times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, is it possible to rephrase your last question in this respect?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've already asked the question. You, yourself, can look at this document once again. Take a look at the fourth paragraph on page 3. The last sentence in that paragraph as is as follows, and I quote: "The attempt to annihilate the Muslim population after the takeover of Srebrenica is the gravest and the most obvious example of genocide during the war in former Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question to the witness is as follows: Is this the analysis referred to by Mr. McCloskey or is it your claim?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just again refer to the Krstic judgement and remind Mr. Tolimir that there were -- men were separated from their families in Potocari and sent by bus to execution sites. So a large number were executed and have later been find -- or exhumed from mass graves and identified through DNA analysis. So there were large killings. Of course, there may also have been some fighting on the way and some battle deaths. But, as I said yesterday, we do not know and you do not know how many were killed in those -- in that -- those combats.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Brunborg, what you've just said implies a new question: This thesis that you have just expounded on, is it your initial assumption from which you started your research? Since, here, in the last sentence, you mention articles written in 1996 and 1997. Take a look at the end of the third paragraph. Thank you. Is this a book or a judgement?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are -- these are two books. The one is the -- by David Rohde: "The End Game," which we referred to previously today. The Honig and Booth is also a book written by them. I don't remember the exact title. These books were, as you know, then written before our -- or my assignment and also before the trials against Krstic and other people accused of -- of war crimes in Srebrenica. Honig and Booth: "Record of a war crime."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we see the title on the list of references, yeah, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And -- thank you, Your Honour. And also we see the full title of the book by David Rohde: "End Game: The Betrayal and Fall of Srebrenica: Europe's worst massacre since World War II."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Correct me if I'm wrong, but my understanding of your testimony is that your article was informed by the decision and conviction on genocide in the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Are you aware that before that case, there is other judgements of this Tribunal at Appeals level confirming a genocide tried in another tribunal like this one in ICTR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe the Krstic case was the first case where an accused was found guilty of being involved in genocide. As far as I know, it was the first genocide case of -- in Europe since World War II. But, as you also know, at the ICTR in Arusha there had been already genocide cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes, my question is: Was your article informed by that decision of the ICTR, which ultimately came to the Appeals Chamber as was confirmed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Krstic case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: No, Akayesu case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ICTR?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so. Excuse me, since we were talking here about genocides in Europe, not in Africa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. For the record, I have to say, that this report by General Delic is 1D373. And I quoted it because it's absolutely in contradiction with what this witness is saying about the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Its own commander is saying something else. It is 1D373 for the record. And now can we have P1776. That's a report dating from 2009. Can we see page 38 in Serbian, and page 34 in English. What we want to look at here is addendum 2 to your report entitled: "Definitions of terms in relation to victims of Srebrenica." Here, you define the term of a disappeared person as the place and date of disappearance. So you define this as a date when this person went missing, or, rather, when this person was last seen alive, and then you add that that is not necessarily the date of death. And then in the footnote, you say this could either the date the informant her/himself, last saw the person alive or a date based on information provided by an eye-witness through the informant. This is quite unclear, so I want to ask you the following: This definition of the date when the person went missing, is that the date given by the informant based on his own personal observations, or based on some information received from alleged eye-witnesses? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. We received this information in the -- in the lists of missing and dead persons from ICRC, and we had some contact with ICRC about the interpretation of this question and that's, as far as I remember, they told us this is how this question should be or this information should be interpreted. But we do not know in each case whether it was last seen alive by the family member himself or herself, or by somebody else, or whether it was a known date of death. So we have no information about this. We have not seep this -- the individual reports from the family members of the missing persons. We have only -- all the information we have from them is the date of disappearance interpreted in the way we just described and the place of disappearance, which is also interpreted in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Bearing in mind what you just said, could you tell me: Did you research at all the level of reliability of this information about the date of disappearance?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I do not really see how we could have researched that. Then we would have had to interview family members and we did not have access to the names or where they lived. So that would -- would have been an impossible task. But I can only say that the dates that were reported for missing and the places of disappearance reported as missing are consistent with later findings about exhumed bodies from mass graves and other graves, where the missing persons have been identified as dead. So there is no inconsistency in this. In fact, we deleted cases where the place of disappearance or especially date of disappearance was inconsistent with our criteria, but some of these have later been found identified as dead in Srebrenica-related graves. So we were too strict, one could say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your previous answer, you said that you received the list from the International Committee of the Red Cross, and then I want to ask you: If you didn't talk to those people who reported the missing persons, could you at least analyse the documents that they have given, the documents in which they registered the fact of a missing person? Is there any sort of written trail that you analysed, or did you simply base your work on the lists?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have access to the documents where families reported persons as missing. We only had access to a list of names with dates of disappearance and place of disappearance. And the -- the ICRC would not provide that information to us. They did not even provide all the information in their own lists. They did not give us the information on whether a certain disappearance was related to the fall of Srebrenica. If they had done that, things would have been easier. But in October 2008, ICRC provided the OTP with a list of -- called: "Srebrenica-related Missing Persons," where that -- they had considered the information given by family members on whether -- whether a person disappeared in connection with the fall of Srebrenica. It would have been useful to have had that information before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So does that mean that, for the purposes of your analysis about the demography of war, you only had the list of the persons with the date and place of their disappearance? Was that the sole basis for such an in-depth analysis in which you claim what you claim? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. No, it was not the only sole basis. It was not the sole basis for our claim. First, we had two different lists from ICRC, two different lists from PHR, and then, as we discussed yesterday, we -- we compared these lists with the census of 1991 and found that a large number, almost everybody on the missing lists, also lived in this area in 1991. We also looked at lists of survivors after the war, notably displaced persons, and voters and found very few potential survivors. So -- and we did all kinds of analysis, checking for inaccuracies, correcting inaccuracies when they were obvious. So I think it is wrong to say that we based our analysis solely on these lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Without going into details about the reliability of those lists and how many of those persons were logged in the Federation and how many in Republika Srpska, because it is irrelevant for the purposes of this questioning but it is relevant for the purposes of your research, I'm going to ask to you instead to look at the first paragraph in this report of yours here where we can read the following: "The registers of persons in period between the -- the 1st of July or immediately before but not earlier, the 1st of July, were considered the most relevant" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I have to interrupt you. I don't know where you are reading from. Can you tell us which page and which line again in both languages?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the first paragraph, date of disappearance. I already read the first sentence, and now I'm reading the second sentence. If you found it, I will continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I'm going to read it once again for the record: "Records with the reported disappearance or death, between 11 July and 31st of August, 1995, or immediately before but not earlier than 1st of July, were considered the most relevant. But also records with disappearances between 1st of September and the 31st of December, 1995, from locations in or near the enclave, were included in our analysis."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is as follows: Why did you leave this period open as far as the 31st of December, 1995? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We included a few cases of date of disappearance after 1995 because persons were found -- were said to be disappearing in places that were -- had been defined as Srebrenica-related. And also because the ICRC provided us this list in October 2008 with a number of persons listed as Srebrenica-related, and seven of those were -- had a date of disappearance in 1996. But the date of disappearance for those seven were, in some cases, not complete. So it is possible that they were misprints. The possibility of misprint is -- is everywhere and that is also a reason why we included a few cases of disappearances in -- through May and June, 1995. One of them was not complete. About the -- the 1996 disappearances, three of them -- no. Two out of the seven had -- have later been found in mass graves and identified as dead. Of those in May and June, one has been found as identified as dead. So we -- we cannot -- we used different information. If I may come back to your -- your previous question on whether we based our analysis solely on these lists, I would say that, later findings have confirmed our preliminary conclusions and the later findings are based on exhumations and DNA analysis and identification of dead. They are all supported our first conclusions in 2005 and -- and the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is this: If you take into account such a wide spectrum much events and activities and move the deadline to the end of 1995 and even if you take all of those killed, irrespective of how they were killed, would then all such victims be victims of the genocide, as defined in your report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not go into the details or -- about whether each individual was part of a genocide or not. Our genocide conclusion is based on the Krstic findings, the judgement, I mean, and I don't know if they -- or I don't think the Judges considered each and every missing or dead person in the genocide connection. They had an overall impression of events, and that's what we based our conclusion on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: A moment ago, I quoted General Delic's report drafted on the very day of the breakthrough from the RS to the Federation. There were witnesses here who stated that they carried their own dead from the location of Baljkovica from the RS to Federation territory once the corridor was opened up. They also said that the entire unit pulled out, including the dead they carried alongside. Would all those dead, too, be included among the victims of genocide?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: If these deaths were reported by the families as missing, they would be included; otherwise, not. It is possible that some of them were returned to the families and then the families had no need to report their relatives as missing. But I don't have any detailed information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Who could provide us with that information if not you? You seem to have taken into account all sorts of victims as victims of genocide. You all put them in the same basket. How are we supposed to sort it out here before this Tribunal? Perhaps you have a proposal for us.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as I said a few minutes ago, we did not take each and every -- consider each and every missing or dead person in the genocide context. We described in the academic article a -- events that resulted in a large number of killed persons. That is certain. And other people, other authors, have described this as a genocide, and the Judges in the Krstic trial and other trials have also described this as a genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yesterday, at page 8, you discussed some figures you established. You put forth the figure of 7.905. Do you recall that particular number?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you recall whether there was a single death reported to you that didn't make it on this list of 7.905?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Many, in fact, several hundred. One is listed in Table 12 of the -- our 2009 report, and in the one of the exhibits yesterday, where there was inclusive -- not conclusive evidence. For example, the ICMP has in -- found 281 cases of unique profiles, DNA profiles that were linked to missing persons, but they could not defined [sic] which person the unique profile can be associated with, because, say, siblings or fathers and sons have such similar DNA profiles that it was not possible to, say, link the DNA profile based on bones to -- to the family members that have reported and have donated blood. An extreme example is twins, male twins in this case. Twins have -- monozygotic twins have identical DNA. So you cannot know if you find, then, bones with a profile; that is, matches, a twin. You cannot tell whether it is -- which of the twins it is associated with. You cannot tell which body it is. So that's why there are deaths that are at the current state excluded, because it is not certain which persons they can be associated with. There are also several hundred -- I -- persons or profiles, DNA profiles of persons that have not been able to link to any name, no-name profiles. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies, Your Honours. Mr. Tolimir is not receiving interpretation at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could it perhaps -- Mr. Tolimir, when I'm talking to you, do you understand me now? Do you receive interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I can hear you now. It was my mistake, because I seem to have to push the switch and toggle the channels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Last sentence of the witness was: "There are also several hundred persons or profiles, DNA profiles of person that have not been able to link to any name, no-name profiles." And then Dr. Hagland [sic] wanted to continue with a word, "Perhaps" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, not Dr. Hagland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was a big mistake. We have had so many witnesses here in the Tribunal that it occurs that -- and I apologise for that. Dr. Brunborg, please continue with your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. There were -- these no name DNA profiles cannot be associated with any name, because they were probably people who did not report their family members as missing, either because the whole family was exterminated or they, for medical or political or ethical or some other reasons did not report the person as missing, did not come forward to donate blood or they lived in Australia or a far away country. So I could say since Mr. Tolimir asked are there any death that are not included in a list of 7.905, yes, there are several. No name, DNA profiles, excluded deaths because their DNA profile may be associated with several persons, that also excluded persons as missing because they may be survivors, potential survivors although that is not clear. So, in the -- to conclude, in the 7.905, there are excluded deaths and there are excluded missing persons. Moreover, since we finished this report in April 2009, the OTP has received several hundred DNA profiles identified from the ICMP. So the number is now both missing and of dead is now probably significantly higher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Brunborg. You have just discussed some cases that were still open at the time which may have been resolved in the meantime. Let me ask you this: Do you know when the attack on Srebrenica in July 1995 began, on what date?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember reading books and articles on this, 12 or 13, 14 years ago. It was at the beginning of July 1995, and it culminated with the exodus, large exodus of persons from -- from Srebrenica, the town of Srebrenica, either to Potocari or through the forests. I don't remember the exact date, was it 4th or 5th of July or something? I don't recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that before the VRS entered Srebrenica, the Army of the Federation had already begun their breakthrough from Susnjari, in Jaglici, and that the population had already left for the base in Potocari? Do you recall on what date that was as compared with the entry of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: A gross misstatement of the facts. That's particularly a problem with a witness who may not be associated with those facts. Because how is he to answer a falsely fact-based question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The previous question and the answer of the witness made clear that he was not present during the events. He was tasked with his report and his research much later after the events. He was not an eye-witness. I think it is not necessary to put these kind of questions to the witness. You should ask other witnesses who have been present at that point in time in this area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, these questions are essential, because the witness took it upon himself to research a whole spectrum of missing persons within a very large segment of time, and I'm trying to find out whether he knows the sequence of events which were important for his analysis, unless you deem it unimportant. I'll abide by your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We will not get valid answers to that from the witness. He made clear that he even doesn't know that he -- he didn't have a reason to know when the attack on the enclave commenced. What is the purpose of such a kind of question about the events on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The purpose of this question is for the witness to tell us why, as the date of disappearance, he chose the period between the 1st of August and the 31st of December, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is a very good question. I think the witness should answer this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was given the task, the dates were defined by the OTP and Mr. McCloskey's team. If you look at the chart, 2A in our 2009 report, you will see that the vast majority of the dates of disappearance were in mid-July. On the 11th of July, there were 2.278; 12th, 1.532; 13th, 1.706; 14th, 538; and then it drops. On the 15th, 241; on the 16th, 124; et cetera. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be, of course, helpful to have that shot on the screen. You say this is ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Figure 2A, page 15 in the English version of the report, 2009 report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we have it on the screen disappearing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You haven't told us the basis of your decision to choose those particular dates. My question was what was the basis of your choice by which you decided to include the period between the 11th of July all the way until late December?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness told it was not his choice by the choice of the OTP. Witness, were you given reasons for this decision by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was given -- they told the story about the events, about the losses [Realtime transcript read in error "buses"], about the executions, what was known at that time. And, indeed, when we started looking at the data and made charts such as 2A in the report and also Figure 1 on the previous page, you see that the vast majority of people went missing in the first days of 11th of July and the following four, five days. And that the number of people went missing after July in the rest of 1995 is very minimal. We also see, if you could look -- yeah, there we see in Figure 1 we see there are very few who went missing, reported missing in August, September, October, November, December, almost negligible. If you had deleted those from our analysis it wouldn't have made much impact. But we thought it was fair to include them because some of the reasons for -- for such late dates of disappearance could be misprints or other reasons. We also notice that on Figure 2B on the next page, which we just saw, if you could switch to 2B, please, on page 15 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will come up soon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We see -- thank you. In 2A, we had a total number missing. In 2B, the identified dead has been shaded, and indeed the majority of persons who went missing on those days in July have been identified as dead. So this confirms the -- you say the advice of the OTP that concentrate on those dates. Indeed, those people have been found to be -- found in mass graves and are identified as dead. The exact date of death cannot be -- usually not be found from exhumations, of course, so the exact date of death must be inferred from eye-witnesses and other reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I should make one correction in the record. Page 30, line 10, you are recorded having said: "They told the story about the events, about the buses, about the executions ..." I think you said "about the losses."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On page 30?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No -- on the record. Don't look into the -- no, the record of today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are recorded in line 10 about having said "about the buses," but I think I heard you saying "about the losses."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By the buses, I'm not quite sure, but I think ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You can't see it. It disappeared from the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I said buses, I meant the bussing of men from Potocari to execution sites that is known by witness statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You said "buses" and not "losses," yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I read the relevant part: "Yes, I was given -- they told the story about the events, about the buses, about the executions, what was known at that time." What did you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course, are you right. It should be "losses."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, did you receive any data from the OTP about how many people were killed in combat in the enclave between the 1st and 11th of July which is the period you have just discussed? Were you provided that information or not?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do all those who were killed between the 1st of July and the 11th of July figure in your reports as genocide victims?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, we do not use the term "genocide victim" at all. Secondly, if there were people who were known to be -- to have been killed in combat or otherwise between the 1st and 11th of July, they may not have been reported as missing or dead. To what extent they were not reported, I do not know, but people were not supposed to report those they knew were dead already. Third, there are 41 persons listed as -- with a date of disappearance between the 1st and the 11th of July. Of these -- of those who went missing, the largest group is on the 10th -- 10th of July. Of these, 65.8 per cent have been identified as dead, found in -- in -- exhumed from graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In your report, when deciding on the place of disappearance, you understand it to be the place where the person was last seen alive; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may usually be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It is page 38 in the B/C/S and 34 in the English, in his report.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, page 38 -- oh, sorry, 34. It could or could not be the place of -- of death or it could also be last seen alive. Family members are likely to have reported differently, based on their knowledge about -- about what happened to their relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on what you wrote, I'd like to ask you this: Would it not have been more fair to say that that place was the place where the person reporting that there was a person missing saw that person for the last time? Would that have been the more fair way, to put it that way? Or to take the place of disappearance as the place where the person who last saw somebody alive and then conveyed that information to the person reporting the missing person, would it not have been the more fair way to put it that like that than to say that they disappeared at a location which is, say, 50 or 60 kilometres away?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier, I think there's a mixture of -- of different interpretations of the place of disappearance, unfortunately. We would have liked very much to have a clear definition. In some cases, relatives saw a person dying. In other cases, and if I'm being a family member I'm perhaps reporting that person missing or dead, her or himself. In other cases they heard it from others that the person had died in other cases. Again, a -- they knew that the person was seen in a certain place and that -- that was reported as the last place of -- or as the place of disappearance. So based on -- since we only have a place, a place name, and no interpretation of -- or clear definition of what the meaning of that is for each and every missing person that we have -- we have sort of a bag of different definitions and we have to remember that when we do the analysis that this is not the precise definition, just as the date of disappearance is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you clarify something for me, please. In footnote 23, on page 38 of your report in the B/C/S, which is page 34 in the English version, you discuss the collecting of information on the missing persons by the ICRC. In the last sentence you say: "However, the ICTY -- however this information was not provided to ICTY for the missing persons." Can you clarify that for us, please?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. In the same footnote, it says that the PHR asked this specific question, did he or she disappear after the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995? And that information was provided to us. But ICRC did not pose any precise question to the informants about this, but they based -- they -- they registered the stories of the informants or the interview with an informant, starting with during the fall of Srebrenica or after the fall of Srebrenica, et cetera, et cetera. But this information was not provided to us, so we don't know. We were told that this was the context of the interviews with the family members reporting the missing persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we must have the first break now. And we will resume at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Our apologies for the delay. We had another meeting and a matter to discuss. Mr. Tolimir, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Brunborg, can you please tell us something about your report from 2009. Page 77 in English and 81 in the Serbian. This is the matching up of the OTP list with the list of the International Red Cross. We're looking at paragraph 4 on this page. The third and the fifth paragraph. In the third paragraph you say, I quote: "Although the exact criteria that the ICRC used to select records for this list are not known to us, it is likely that they used the information concerning the circumstances of disappearance reported by the relatives of the missing and being part of the ICRC tracing requests." Then in paragraph 5 you say: "Also, 98 records were included on the 2005 OTP list but were not listed on the ICRC Srebrenica 2008 update. However, on the basis of DNA identification by ICMP and a surmised difference in the understanding of 'Srebrenica related,' we see no reason to exclude these records." In view of this, what are these surmised differences that you are understanding here and that you saw no reason to exclude?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't remember each of these 1998 records, but, as it says, they were not included in the ICRC Srebrenica 2000 [sic] update. But they were included, they have been identified as dead, and since there have been exhumed from Srebrenica-related graves, identified as dead, that is the reason why we thought they could safely be included. If they had not been found in Srebrenica-related graves, we probably would not have included them. But to give a definite answer to that, I would have to look at all those 1998 records again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Dr. Brunborg, just one clarification for the record. You were talking about the ICRC Srebrenica 2008 update; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As you say in your report, the criteria were not clear to you either. So my question is: Why did you then use the ICRC lists in order to draft the OTP lists when you working in the OTP? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we trust that ICRC collected good information on the circumstances of missing persons and the place of disappearance and the date of disappearance, et cetera, and ICRC, being a neutral humanitarian organisation, would have no reason to misrepresent the data in any way. Remember also, that the basis for the ICRC -- the main basis for their collection of missing data is tracing missing relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of your answer, my question, then, is: Does that mean that you did not check the authenticity of the data that was provided to you by the ICRC in those lists? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The authenticity was verified by -- by the owner and provided by the data -- the ICRC. We could not check the authenticity of each and every record in any other way than what we have described earlier by checking consistency, removing duplicates, looking for survivors, checking, especially, that is important, with the census 1991 to see if the data was correct. To see that the dates of birth and name, et cetera, of the missing persons were, indeed, were correct and as recorded in 1991, four years before they went missing. But, as I said earlier, we did not have access to the document, the handwritten document, we believe, for each missing person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have the Prosecutor's material that referred to events, activities, and testimonies on the basis of which parameters could be accessed that speak differently? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please be a little more specific in that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If you worked only on the basis of the lists which you trusted and relied on, did you have any other documents from the OTP for whom you drafted the report in order to check the veracity of those lists?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We only had documents describing what was going on, the events in those days. I don't remember which. They were not very important, and we had, of course, then -- we had a list of places of disappearance that were Srebrenica related. This list was drawn up by the OTP, by people who were very familiar with events in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: For example, we have just read Delic's report which was created on the last day when the Army of Republika Srpska opened the corridor for them to be able to leave Republika Srpska, because they were trying to get through in the middle of battle. There are no -- there is no -- there are no figures for losses in the B and H army but there is information for the VRS casualties. There was another witness here who testified, who stated information that there were 900 or more persons who were killed in the column as the column was trying to get through, out of the area. As a demographer, did you take into account this fact about these 900 persons, and did you take into account the fact that they were killed in battle and not in any other way? Did you use all of those things in order to complete the information?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said previously, we relied on data on individuals, missing and dead persons, needing last name and date of birth, et cetera of each person. So a given number of 900 persons would not -- could not be used by us unless accompanied by a list of those 900 persons. Whether you are claiming that those 900 were killed in battle that is not -- I don't have any expertise on that, but that may be an exaggeration.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm just saying what your colleague, Dusan Janc, who was a witness for the Prosecution said and to whom you referred. But I am saying is if you had information that there was a breakthrough attempt at Baljkovica and that a certain number of persons were killed, why did you exclude that piece of information in your report and include them in the total figure for those who were killed in the genocide?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I'm not sure if it is correct to say that Witness Dusan Janc was a colleague of the current witness. He explained the relation between staff members of the OTP and his involvement earlier. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, he certainly never said 900 people were killed in combat either, so, I, again, object to the misstatement of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir. But, sorry for interrupting, you. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes, can you just assist me at page 59, lines 5 to 6, you have just stated: "I don't have any expertise on that, but that may be an exaggeration." How do you come to the conclusion, since you don't have the expertise, that that could be an exaggeration? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I've seen and heard. I've looked at Mr. Janc's report, not having saw it in detail, but as Mr. McCloskey just said, he did not say that all these or -- were killed in battle. And what I know, then, is that many of those people who went through the forest were found in mass graves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Brunborg, this is a report by Dusan Janc on the surface remains that were found on the road from Srebrenica to Baljkovica. My legal assistant is going to find the reference for you because the Prosecutor asked that we give you the reference. All I'm asking you is this: Did you have any knowledge about any surface remains of victims, remains that were found on the surface? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is just what may be a translation issue, but I'm sure the General will agree there is not a road from Srebrenica to Baljkovica, and so I think he is referring to surface remains, not along the road. Because that is a very important distinction in this case, found along the road or found in the woods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, would you agree with that statement of Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do agree, Mr. President. I said "surface remains." I didn't say on the road. Perhaps I did say it, perhaps it was an error in translation. I don't want to blame the interpreters, perhaps I did misspeak. But this is not what I meant to say. I'm talking about surface remains. They're even showing a table here where the route is indicated, and there are red dots pointing out where the remains were found, and we will show that during this testimony. I apologise to Mr. McCloskey if we misunderstood one another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps you said on the way from Srebrenica to Baljkovica, which could mean also the word. And now, please, your answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we started this work in 1999/2000, we had no information on particular surface remains. We knew there were some, but, at that time, very few had been identified. For the current report of 2009, we have included in Table 4 exhumation sites. Table 4, page 8 and 9 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we're not going to go into that any more until I bring up the requested information. I'm asking you this now: Why did the demographers, while calculating the killed and the missing in relation to Srebrenica, also count those who were missing in Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because date of disappearance and place of disappearance was -- were conveyed to us as relevant to the fall of Srebrenica. So Zepa was then one of the places, I believe, I don't remember all the names, but one of the places that was -- that we were told was related to the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if there were any victims or casualties in Zepa at all during the combat; and if there were any, do you know how many? Thank you. Well, perhaps it would be more proper for me to show you Table 6B on page 19 in the Serbian, this is page 17 in the English, then you can also use those tables. Because I don't want any kind of answer. I would like to have a precise answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to your first question, whether we had information about deaths in combat, no. As I repeatedly say, we did not. And the Table 6B which you pointed, there were -- 35 people have been identified as dead with place of disappearance being Zepa out of a total of 89 people being listed as last seen or with place of disappearance being Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You established that as the place of disappearance, but in Zepa everybody was present. All the parties to the conflict and UNPROFOR and all the witnesses that came here who were active participants in the events did not see any dead. Are these accurate data, then, and can they undermine the overall results in that case of your records?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I do not have any information about events in Zepa or the situation in Zepa in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But you have just said that 89 persons were seen in Zepa for the last time. And, according to the definitions you established for the needs of this analysis, that is the last place where they were seen. So that means that they disappeared in that place. Yes or no? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: They either disappeared in that place or they were last seen alive in that place, according to the family members of the missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And do family members go to war with soldiers? Do you have any grounds to assert that they were in Zepa when they weren't in Zepa? Are there any documents that would show that they were actually in Zepa or is this just on the basis of hearsay? Do you have any kind of reports or statements from those persons that you then used for the purposes of your analysis? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know that family members stated that their relatives were last seen in Zepa, whether that information is based on their own -- what they saw themselves or through somebody else, I do not know, since we do not have exact information about the basis for the relatives' statements about place of disappearance. It could be that they had the information from other people who were together with the missing persons and who survived. That is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But these 89 persons are listed as missing persons. Have you asked the OTP if they have any information about the disappearance of these people, on the basis of those reports where it is indicated that Zepa is their place of disappearance? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And I don't know if OTP knows anything about this. But what we do know -- the hard fact is that 35 of these people have been found as dead in mass graves or exhumed from mass graves or other grave-sites. A separate analysis could be done of those disappearing in Zepa and where they were found later in -- in graves. But that information is not included here. Then we'd have to do, as I said, a separate analysis of these 35 according to exhumation sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If the brigade in Zepa, the civilian authorities in Zepa, the army in Zepa, the UNPROFOR in Zepa, none of them recorded 89 killed or dead in Zepa - the OTP didn't record them either - how can we understand, then, the figures that you provided here, based on -- an analysis based on that information?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I ask you, where do the 35 dead people come from? They were reported as missing in Zepa. So it is very strange that they were not -- no deaths were seen, but I do not know anything about events in Zepa and what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I would be all too glad to answer your question if I had the right to answer questions here. But since you use this in your report, I'm simply trying to find out from you how can I find it so that I can clarify it for myself. My following question: Can you explain us why did you include in the list of missing persons related to Srebrenica those people who went missing after they were at Baljkovica? That's the place that Delic is referring -- is referring to when he says that his army managed to link up with other forces, that they are still carrying out combat activities, that they captured eight members of VRS. So why did you include those people when it is possible that they are persons who died in combat, and, furthermore, in the territory under the control of the ABiH? Why did you include those people into the lists of victims from Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we were asked to make a -- complete lists of missing and dead persons related to the fall of Srebrenica. We were not asked to distinguish between or trying to separate out combat deaths. If there were information about that, then I'm sure OTP would have taken care of that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If that was your goal in writing the report, then maybe, to be acceptable, if the OTP was really set out to resolve this problem. But you wrote your report for this Court and this is what you're testifying about. So that's why I want you to tell this Court and explain it -- explain to this Court why did your interview include these people from Baljkovica? We've heard people -- testifying here who said there were 40 dead people on Serbian side and that the members of the BiH army carried away their dead casualties. Why did you include those people in the list of persons missing in Srebrenica? I am satisfied with your answer, if you simply say, Well, that's the task that was assigned to us by the Prosecution. It's all right with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't know of anything in the record that indicates there's been Muslims in the -- at battle at Baljkovica that have been reported missing. So he is making that conclusion. If that's his position, okay, but if he is referring to it as some conclusion he needs to point to the record because I don't think it's such a thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Brunborg, do you recall the question of Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he gave the answer himself very well. That was the task assigned to us by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We are satisfied with the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm going to move over to the next topic. Yesterday, we talked about the lists drafted by the BiH army. Can we have page 104 in Serbian and 97 in English. I'm talking about the Exhibit P1 -- P07170. Thank you. Okay. We have it here. This table shows discrepancies between several reports. For instance, the date of death as reported by BiH and the date of death as reported by the Prosecution. So here can you see 220 cases - can we zoom in - 220 cases which do not correspond to the Prosecution list in 2005. And we see that they died before the events related to the fall of Srebrenica, and yet their bodies were identified by DNA and found in the mass graves that the Prosecution is linking up with the fall of Srebrenica. They died before the fall of Srebrenica and, yet, here, their bodies were identified and they were found in the mass graves. And it is the BiH army that reported that they lost their lives before the combat that led to the fall of Srebrenica. My question is then: Can you explain this table to us? And can you give us some explanation for this phenomenon that in the Prosecution list and in the mass graves we found names of people who died before the fall of Srebrenica in 1992, 1993 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you give your answer, just for the record, this is not P7170 but 65 ter 07170. It was already received as an exhibit, and a later stage the Registrar will provide everybody with correct numbers by sending out a memorandum.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for clarity of the record, this document was assigned Exhibit P1776 yesterday on the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
