utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is the original report of the -- I didn't know that. The original report of the witness. Dr. Brunborg, now your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, the answers to your question is given on page 95 of the same report in the English version. See if you could see that, please. For these 220 inconsistent records, we sent -- we sent the lists to the Bosnian Army and got their responses that 140 have been confirmed as identified and related to Srebrenica grave-sites by the ICMP. So even though their reported dates by ABiH was inconsistent, then they have, nevertheless, been found in Srebrenica-related grave-sites. 127 of the total 220 have been corrected by the Ministry of Defence in response to the OTP request for clarification and the corrected dates of death and the additionally provided place of deaths clearly point to the fact that these were all Srebrenica victims. But, finally, there are 38 cases out of the 220 that remain undecided. For the 31 out of these 38 cases, the OTP has requested such a clarification, and the results are expected very soon. It is written here. I'm not clear whether we have received a response to that or not. So the conclusion is that although initially the date of death or date of disappearance seemed in consistent with the fall of Srebrenica clarification by the Ministry of Defence and findings by the ICMP find that most of these 220 are, indeed, Srebrenica related. The reason again being that there are often misprints in reports for various reasons and so when you have several information sources and one of them may be inconsistent with the others, but if the overwhelming majority of the information shows in a certain direction, we tend to rely on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Brunborg, can you tell me, when we talk about the registers of deaths in ABiH, do they make the entries whenever they want or do they make the entries when the actual death occurred or at least in the year when the actual death occurred? So is it possible to now -- to change those registers now based on the DNA data simply because somebody is saying that they haven't died in 1992, 1993, 1994. I mean, if we know there are grave-sites, how can we now change the date of death simply based on this additional information? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I'm not familiar with the proceedings of the Bosnian Army with regard to recording of deaths. But I think that the procedures are also not perfect, like all procedures for such things have sometimes -- are imperfect and sometimes lead to errors, especially in difficult war situation. Moreover, many of the reported deaths in the ABiH records are not combat deaths. They are also deaths from natural reasons because of pension rights for -- for family members, so -- and many of those reported deaths in the ABiH records were not working or not participating in combat. They were not soldiers but civilians working in the civilian operations of the army or the non-combat operations. So I think that this is not a problem that further investigations saw that there -- there have been some mistakes in the first round of recording. To repeat, in a war situation the date of death is often not very well known.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for this explanation. So, first of all, does that mean that it has been determined that certain administrative services within the army or civilian protection or the TO or wherever else, deliberately gave false information in order to gain certain material advantage related to pensions and similar entitlements? Were there such cases?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not claiming that, but -- and I don't know any -- have any evidence for claiming that. But it's a fact that people sometimes present data in a way that is economically favourable to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When we are talking about economically favourable things, were such economically favourable things used in relation to the registers of persons missing in Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us then get back to the Table 6.4 which relates to those 220 cases whose date of death does not correspond with the Prosecution list of missing persons from Srebrenica compiled in 2005. We have it here on the screen now. Let us take the fifth entry, Hasanovic. You can see clearly here 1992 or more precisely, 1805992. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does that mean that he went missing in 1992?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: DOD here probably means date of death. But I am -- yes, that's what I think it believes. Not date of disappearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. So if he died in 1992 his family surely knows that. How is it possible that he appears here in this register as a victim of an event that took place in July 1995 in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you understand, I'm not familiar with this case here. I assume that he was found in a -- in a mass grave or a -- a grave, together with Srebrenica-related victims, and so the ICMP concluded that he died in connection with fall of Srebrenica. Moreover, he was reported to the ICRC as missing by their -- by their relatives. ICMP has made an investigations to find out whether there were a mixture of old deaths and more recent deaths in graves and they have found apparently a few cases where there were both deaths from 1992 and 1995 and I think in Bratunac, but I'm not a specialist on this. And I don't know if there were such mixed bodies in Orahovac. But, anyway, it seems like ICMP has concluded that this was a person who died with -- in connection with the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For a better understanding, could you perhaps help me. In the headline, we see there in the fourth column, DOB and then in brackets OTP. What does DOB --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Date of birth. Date of birth and then DOD here probably means date of death. And this Hasanovic, the military has not corrected that date of death. I don't know if that person is included or not. But below, there is one who is listed with a date of death 10th of January, 1994, but this has been corrected to 12th of July [Realtime transcript read in error "January"], 1995, by the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The way the -- the -- the date is listed is strange. Can you explain that for this person? It is 1805992, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the way -- same way as the identification numbers in the former Yugoslavia were recorded, date of birth, with day and month, and year having three digits but not the century. 992, not 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. In line 6, page 51, just now you say: "But this has been corrected to 12th January 1995 by the military."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 12th July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: 12th July 1995. By which military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- the army -- the Ministry of Defence of the Bosnian federal -- Federation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, does this point to the possibility that this list may have been manipulated by the clerks working in the ministry and in the military as well as people who reported the missing persons? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. That is an accusation that I cannot support.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Take a look at the ninth line. It's the second Avdic surname, Avdic, Avdulah. You can see that his date of death is 10th of January, 1994. How is it possible for him to be included in the people who died in Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is, in fact, the eighth line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as can you see in one of the further columns, the clarification has been requested. So this is inconclusive. This is -- the evidence is not so strong here, so I think I need to check whether this was included or not. But there are -- the evidence is inconclusive here. And the date -- the death of this person has not been confirmed. There's no yet any DNA analysis connected with this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Take a look at the next person. That person died on the 19th of February, 1993. And you consider this person to be a victim related to Srebrenica. And then two lines down, Salihovic, number 12 and 13. And it is also 94. And then the following one, Alic, again 94. Death is listed as the year of death.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I am very pleased that you pointing out the thoroughness of our work. We first included these people as missing, because we had information from the ICRC and other sources that they had been listed as missing. We are using all available data to check whether the information on -- on the missing with regard to place and date of death is really consistent with the events. And we checked 220 people from the -- from the Army of Bosnia, the Federation, and found 220 cases with inconsistent dates. After further work and checking, we remained with 38. And it remains to be seen if any of these will be excluded or not. So, again, we are looking at all possible inconsistencies. And if you really find evidence for inconsistent place or date of death, we exclude them, of course, from -- from persons having died in connection with the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For my understanding, can you help me? Can I take it from your answer that those who are listed in the military list have died 1993, 1992, 1994, and you have no other lists with different data. Then you excluded them from the whole list of death and missing persons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I need to check this further whether they have actually been excluded or are sort of on the waiting-list, potential candidates for being excluded or not. But after this thorough search, we remained with only 38 possible inconsistencies and when this is resolved they will either be excluded or included depending on the outcome of the investigations. I will check, Your Honour, whether they have been excluded so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I need a clarification for the relation between the different columns. We see the military entries in column 5 with some dates before the event in Srebrenica. Then we see the date of death corrected, all dates in July 1995. And then we -- at the end, we have a list of the -- the sites of mass graves. Could you please explain what does that mean, if a person is listed in the military list of the ABiH, for instance, to have died in 1992, and then found on Cancari Road, for instance. This is Hilmo Arnaut. What is your finding, the final finding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I said, I'm not familiar with the way the deaths were reported to military, whether it was done by families or the army itself, but the data here indicate that there have been some mistakes in their reporting and whether that is due to typos or systematic fraud or other errors, I don't know. I need to go and check the correspondence and communications with the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The military list, if you look at this column, you see very often the date of the 10th of January, 1994. Have you any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That is -- what is often used when an exact date of birth or of an event in a year is not known, 1st of January is often used instead, and it could be here it has been twisted and 10th of January has been listed instead. That is a possibility. First of the month or 1st of January is, as I said, often used as a placement, an indication that they don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But here it is always the 10th of January.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there are some 1st of January also. If you look at number approximately 15, Jusic, Akija Jusic [phoen] -- no, Kandzetovic, who died on the 1st of January, 1994. But there are many on the 10th. Whether that is related to a special event on the 10th of January, 1994, or some kind of misreporting or use of 10th of January instead as an unknown, indication of an unknown date, I don't know. We would need to clarify that with the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Just a clarification, maybe two. At page 54, lines 15 to 6, you have responded: "But the data here indicated that there have been mistakes in their reporting of the date of death," as Judge Fluegge has just been asking you. Have you considered the possibility that there was no mistake that the information in the data is, in fact, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But when we -- we found inconsistencies. Remember that for these people we had information about the day they went missing, received from family members. So depending, should -- who should we believe in? Should we believe in the army data or the family members' data. That's why we requested further clarification from the military. But if it is very obvious that the -- the -- the military data are correct, and in some cases they did not change the date, then, of course, we will accept that and exclude them from Srebrenica deaths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: The second question flows in from that, the one you just answered and this is at page 53, lines 22 to 25. You stated there that: "But after this thorough search, we remained with only 38 possible inconsistencies, and when this" -- I'm missing somewhere: "... they will either be excluded or included, depending on the outcome of the investigations." Do I understand your evidence to mean that they're actually ongoing investigations now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were -- for these -- it says on page 95 in the English version that 31 cases out of 38 already are in the process of clarification. Additional clarification would be requested for the remaining seven cases. So this was -- this was the situation in April 2009. And perhaps this should be written an addendum to this report on the outcome of this clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here, you said that the army may have chosen the date at random. Didn't you know that armies report precise dates of disappearance and that their files are usually more accurate than civilian files? In the army, there has to be a -- a living person registering someone. Is it not more appropriate to have someone on the list by way of a physical report or only by -- by someone -- by mere data?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I did not say that the army chose dates at random. I said that when dates are registered, errors are made, everywhere, in all situations, in all registers. Whether we should rely on physical reports, first, we don't have such physical reports. Secondly, for thousands of people, that would be an impossible task, first to acquire those reports and then to go through them. So we do rely on dates and names, et cetera, hard facts, since we are talking about thousands of persons. That's the only way we could manage to do this analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that in order to have someone deleted from a list, the army would only remove a person from the list provided they have a death certificate. Under the law, all local authorities were duty-bound to issue such death certificates only following an investigation, or, rather, they had to make sure that someone died, indeed.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware there are legal requirements to define somebody as dead. When you said that in order to have someone deleted from a list, just now, I don't know which list you are talking about. Are you talking about the list of missing persons, or deaths or anything else? But, generally, it is often important to have a legal statement saying that a certain person is dead for inheritance and other reasons. Even though a body is not found, in some cases a court may declare a person as dead. But, of course, a body, or, particularly if it is reported by DNA analysis, makes it easier for a court to declare a person as dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Here we have Table 6.4. There are 28 people listed there. According to army files, all of those deaths occurred between 1992 and the 10th of June 1995. That is to say, before the events in Srebrenica. But basically in almost all of the cases, as mentioned by Judge Fluegge as well, you put them on the list. Some of them made it on to the list by DNA analysis found in the grave-sites. So what was more important, was it DNA analysis, reports on grave-sites, or the reports of the army which drafted a list of missing persons on the spot? Because any army considers their personnel the most important asset in a time of war. It is a fighting asset. So which criterion should we rely on?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here I believe it was ICMP that decided that these deaths were Srebrenica related since they were found in graves with many other Srebrenica-related deaths. Consequently, even though they reported date of death was inconsistent, they were accepted by -- well, ICMP did not have that date of death as reported by the army. That is something we found by comparing with army lists. But, anyway, they are found in Srebrenica-related graves, so it is possible, quite likely, that these dates are wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. How will this Court know that they were, indeed, found in those grave-sites and that DNA analysis was not conducted based on fictitious data and reports or that such DNA analysis were not retrieved from other entities and then linked to some of the grave-sites? Did you carry out those checks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is up to the Chamber at the end of this trial to judge which kind of list is reliable and we'll compare, of course, all reports we receive in the evidence we were able to obtain in the courtroom. And this witness is not an expert of the ICMP. Please bear that in mind. You should rephrase your question, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I will. We have many lists of deceased persons, for example, D120. Could we please have page 7 of that document on the screens. Page 5 in B/C/S, 7 in the English version just to give you an illustration of the size or the number of people. I'm simply asking the witness to tell us which criteria we should use when preparing our Defence case. Could we please have D150. Sorry. D -- it's actually 1520. This is an annex to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina guide which had been drafted before the clashes in Srebrenica. Page 5 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is not very satisfactory. We need a real number: P or D, or 65 ter. What is it about? There are millions of documents. Which is the correct number? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's my understanding they've asked to hold this witness over to Monday and a question has -- such as what should he tell him on how to prepare his Defence or how is the Judge to know, these are just so time-wasteful. If they're going to keep him over, can we stop wasting time like that. Unless he is told not to, I'm afraid he is going to continue to do that. So many of his questions are right on the money and he knows what he's doing, so I don't understand why he keeps going off on those directions. It's just a waste of time which we do not have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It was all in good -- with good intensions. Could we please have D120.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is command of the 8th Srebrenica Operations Group number 69, from 1994. Are you really referring to that? This should not be broadcast. It is under seal, I'm told, although it is not mentioned in your list.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then should not be broadcast publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could just have a look at how the lists -- how precise the lists are. For example, the page -- page 5 in B/C/S, and 7 in English. All this was drafted before the fall of Srebrenica. Here we can see page 5 -- item 5. You can see how long the list is and the title states: "Names of soldiers killed up to the 31st of January, 1994." So we have the list, and all of a sudden we have some international organisations meddling with it, and it is from AB and H documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it will be a long question. I would like to ask the witness first: Can you tell us, have you ever seen this list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I have not. They are many names here, and I cannot answer on the spot. We would need to check if any of these names are also on those 220 cases with inconsistent date of death. So I thank you for providing us with this list, Mr. Tolimir. We like such lists because it makes our case stronger. We will -- we can then delete inconsistent cases. However, there is a problem with the list and it has very limited information of names. It has only first name and family name. The father's name is missing, there's nothing on date of birth. So -- and there are many -- there are many people with the same name. There are people in -- they are hundreds of people in Bosnia with the same name. So it's a bit difficult to be conclusive on this. But we'll do our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think, Dr. Brunborg, at the moment you are not engaged with the OTP. Mr. Tolimir, you should use this witness and his expertise during your cross-examination to get as much as possible from him but in relation to his expertise as a demographer. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I wanted to show you just this one page, yet this entire document consists of nothing but names. Now we can go back to page 1 of this same document. My question for you is this: Did you at all rely on the files and lists of those killed before the war in order to ascertain the veracity of reported deaths and the data you received once you realised that there were discrepancies?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we discovered such discrepancies, such deaths are deleted from the list of missing or dead -- missing and dead, in connection with the fall of Srebrenica. We do not rely on such lists if the death -- date of death is different, very different from mid-July 1995. We have no interest in cheating or making out of -- blowing up deaths, missing persons artificially. But my co-author, Ewa Tabeau, will -- and we'll look at this, if it has not been resolved satisfactorily already.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I merely wanted you to tell me whether it is standard practice to check your data against the lists of the army because should someone willingly depart from the army, there are legal consequences for that person. Here we saw the units and lists of all those killed up to 1994, and, as we can see, based on this sheet of paper, it is part of your list. My question, following all this, is: By way of conclusion, is it possible that there were manipulations by the army due to which you decided against using their data and to rely exclusively on ICRC and other sources for -- for data?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, when we started this work in 1999, we did not have any information from the army. But we requested data from the army exactly to do what you have indicated, to check whether some people died before 1995 which would merit exclusion from the lists. That's what we were in the process of doing. We found by checking 220 cases with inconsistent date of death, now after further clarification, 38 remain, and we intend -- and this should also be resolved. I do not see why the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia should have an interest in changing dates incorrectly for a small number. This is, after all, a very small number compared to the total losses in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Brunborg. But we did see on this list here only on one sheet of 29 names that the army data was used in nine cases -- ten. Let's say ten. We've just analysed that. Otherwise, there are still 28 open cases. My question then is this: Why were the files used between 1992 and 1995 used --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand. Could Mr. Tolimir please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the interpreters ask to repeat your last question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Brunborg, tell us, please, why, in these 28 cases there are demands to change army data for 1992 to 1995 so these people were missing in their files for five years and why were there no requests to change ICRC or OTP data which had no corroborating documents, save for simple registrations or reports of missing persons?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I hope we have a translation error, because the requests was never to change numbers. It was a request to clarify. So I'm hoping that's just a translation error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Brunborg.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think Mr. McCloskey said that there was a request to clarify inconsistencies so that we could make -- so that our data material would be as good as possible. And for some cases, the -- they decided the -- they changed the dates; and for other cases they did not change the date. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise to Mr. McCloskey. I believe I said that there were corrections -- or, rather, changes of army data because we see here corrected dates, and I only wanted to be fair to the interpreters. That's why I'm repeating this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Brunborg, can you tell us this, please: How does the ICRC update its lists of missing and killed in Bosnia and Herzegovina; and how do they establish that some of those deaths are Srebrenica related? Because you said that they carry out processes of updating their databases in their computers, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, there were several questions asked at the same time. How -- the first one is how the ICRC updates its lists of missing and killed in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Well, they have an office or more in -- in Bosnia and they receive information from people. They receive new requests from families for missing persons and they also receive information about survivors, really, actually for only 26 people since the beginning of the registration of missing persons. And they also do some technical checks, I believe, and find sometimes mistakes. As I said, there is no perfect organisation. They sometimes -- data are added twice or there are misprints, both in names and date of birth and date of disappearance and so on. And when these errors are discovered, they are corrected. But from 2005 to 2008, they -- one was excluded because for a technical error, for example, excluded by the ICRC. So I'm not saying that every record is absolutely correct but the overwhelming majority is based on the -- on correct data.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could we please have page 44 in e-court of the report, Table 3.1. I will need this in order to put my next question. It is the 1999 report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is P1776.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English version, it is page 40. In the B/C/S, page 44. Thank you. We have it before us. Table 3.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: From the point of view of the ICRC, there were 3.459 Srebrenica-confirmed deaths. However, in your report you state that the persons who were identified was actually 5.061. How do you explain the difference between ICRC data and the data you used for your analysis? That is to say, OTP data.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is related to when the data reported and also to the process about informing families about their -- their dead family members. So that's why this involves courts and it's also a legal process. That is why I believe that ICMP has a -- always a higher number than the ICRC. Remember also they also have different lists of missing persons. ICRC [sic] probably has a higher number of missing persons, Srebrenica-related missing persons, that is, than the ICRC. And there is also question of the date of the report, when did they do the counting of number of confirmed deaths, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it mean that their lists were not as up-to-date as those of the OTP, because there seems to be a large difference, particularly in view of all DNA identifications. And can you tell us who took into account the data belonging to the other organisation? Did the OTP reflect upon ICRC data, or was it the other way around? Which was the prevalent piece of information to be used in the course of analyses?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The OTP has tried to integrate data from both ICRC and from ICMP, at the same time avoiding duplications. So since we have data from two sources, we can have different numbers of the totals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we must have our second break now. You have used, all together, approximately 4 hours and 50 minutes in your cross-examination up to now. I would like to know how much additional time you really need for planning purposes. It is important for the OTP, and I would like to know how much time the OTP needs for re-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will do my utmost to stay with the time we requested originally, which was six hours. I may not be successful, but I will strive to. We will in any case, need at least those six hours and by your leave I may request some additional time, in due course, given the fact that the witness will be here on Monday as well. There were certain answers which were far longer than the questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's the usual experience. Questions have to be longer -- shorter than the answers. In that case, it is obvious that we can't finish with this witness this week. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I shouldn't have, I hope, not more than 30 minutes thus far; probably not even that much. So I don't see a lot at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But, for sure, we can't finish today. So we must now take our second break and we'll resume at quarter past 6.00. It is very unfortunate for you, but there is no other way. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My next question is: If, in one list, the OTP or the ICRC list, persons are mentioned about whose fate the person who is drafting the list has no knowledge of, would it then be correct for these persons to be recorded as missing persons, until their fate is established, rather than victims? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. We have tried to keep to the term "missing or dead persons." We have made a list of missing or dead persons. It is possible that the -- the word -- the term "victims" are used in some instances, but, really, we -- you are right, I think, that the missing or dead is a better term than victim. Now when two-thirds are found in graves, being identified as dead, perhaps it is not so inappropriate to use the term "victim" but, of course, it applies only to those that -- whose fates that been proven.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at P1473, please. Page 77, paragraph 2 in the English, and in the Serbian, it's page 103, paragraph 3. This is a judgement by the District Court in Belgrade, the War Crimes Chamber, in the case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, perhaps you gave a wrong reference. The number of this War Crimes Chamber judgement is P1437. I take it from your own list.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much. I made a mistake. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Page 77, paragraph 2 in the Serbian. Thank you. And page 103, paragraph 3, in the English. We have it now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It states, I'm reading this paragraph in the Serbian: "The court took into account Witness Amor Masovic's explanation provided in the course of the examination, that DNA identification is considered preliminary and identification is only finalised when the victim's family signs the identification record." My question is: When drafting your documents and doing your analysis, did you have access to these identification records and did you take them into account? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we did. That is why some of this is under seal, because the families have not yet -- excuse me. The families have, in some cases, not yet signed, I think. But I did not deal with the ICMP, so I'm not 100 percent sure of it -- of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If the families haven't signed those, as Amor Masovic says, is this then considered to be a preliminary rather than the finalised identification until the family signs it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I understand, the DNA identification is final, in that there's -- there's no doubt on behalf of ICMP that there's a match between the different DNA profiles. But from a more legal perspective, then it is considered preliminary. So, for our purpose, this is very useful and important information to have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And does this then avoid possible manipulation whereby somebody could put somebody on that list who -- as being in the mass grave; whereas, they actually died in 1992. Is this possible?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, the ICMP works according to international -- very strict standards, and so there is a -- there are international experts working for ICMP overseeing the operations. They also have, I believe, ways of distinguishing between bodies of -- that died many years apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And was an analysis conducted in any of the cases or a particular check of this data? Are you aware of anything like that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more specific, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was there a check or a comparison made between the finalised records, on the basis of DNA, and those on the basis of other documents that, for example, was -- were based on information from the ICRC, from family members, or the Tribunal? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. We compared all this. And several tables in our report shows these results of comparing ICMP data, identifications with ICRC, our previous lists, et cetera. This is in -- in -- shown in several of the tables in the report, including Tables 5 and many others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Tolimir, the witness has explained this process yesterday during examination-in-chief in detail, and he repeated that today. If you have further questions to clarify some topics that is, of course, helpful, but just to -- to repeat a question, it is not that -- brings us nowhere. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't repeating it. I was just asking whether data from the family, for example, if they buried somebody in 1992 would that now to be corrected pursuant to the DNA that was found in 1998, let's say, in Kozluk, for the sake of an example. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you also again repeat your question in a sort of specific way?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was the main criteria for matching the data of the ICRC, the DNA analysis -- I'm sorry, I'm thinking of the ICMP and their DNA testing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, I'm not a specialist on DNA testing. They run their own operations at very high standards. They have error rates of one in 10.000, so you could expect less than one error of those sample of 8.000 that we are talking about here. And when they have -- are satisfied about an identification, they -- with a given name, they -- they include case numbers, et cetera, and we receive reports. And we compare that report with our reports on missing persons. And -- yeah, that's what I can say. But if we discover they're widely different data on -- on disappearance, we will not, of course -- not exclude and we do exclude some -- some cases, which is -- which shows in -- if you may go quickly through it. Let me see. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm afraid that we're going to lose time. We still have just 15 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, if you look at Table 12 in our report which was shown as one of the exhibits yesterday, you will see that we excluded 12 potential survivors. We -- there some we did not exclude at all, 281. So we are -- we are, indeed, looking at all the data that we are receiving from ICMP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is, again, P1776.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Since we do have P1776 on the screen, and having heard what the witness said, can we now look at page 47 in the Serbian; paragraph 6. And page 43 in English. Page 47 in the Serbian, please. Thank you. P1776, the report from 2009. Can we have that? And page 47 in the Serbian, because what I'm seeing here is page 46. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's e-court page 48. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: E-court numbers not always are the same as the pages in the document. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I don't see the transcript in front of me right now, but we're talking about the report from 2009, P1776.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will put the question while we're waiting, and then if it is something that is disputed, we'll look at it. Anyway, I quote: "As soon as the matching is established, the findings are sent to the pathologist who, if he believes it is correct, would sign the certificate of death." My question is: Could you please explain or clarify to us the procedure, since Amor Masovic spoke about the identification reports that are signed by the family, and you're talking about certificate of death. So what is irregular here? Is it necessary to have both signatures by the pathologist and also by the members of the family, in order to confirm that a person has been identified? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not a specialist on this. Ewa Tabeau had the dealings with the ICMP. ICMP -- I don't know if they're a witness in this case. But there may be a difference here between --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau will testify next week.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. So you can explain then why what is the difference between the signature of a pathologist and the family. There could be legal reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We will ask Ms. Ewa.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at -- we'll leave this for Ewa, then, this complete set of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And I have discussed this with Mr. Gajic. At this point, I don't really see a need to duplicate the efforts and call Ms. Tabeau, and so we were, especially because we don't -- shouldn't create a gap, we were thinking of not calling her unless, of course, material comes up that Dr. Brunborg cannot answer. But -- so I just wanted to let you know that, and Mr. Parsons from ICMP is scheduled for the week of 21 February that will have the answers for the ICMP issues. But, of course, Ms. Tabeau is here and always available for the Defence or the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that precisely this answer by the witness indicates that it is necessary to call Ms. Ewa Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In order to establish the age group, you gave them special names. You used the terms boys and young men. My question is: Was this something that was as a result of a suggestion from the investigator or is it usual in demographics to use these terms, boys and young men? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. That is a common terminology, not only in demography but in other fields as well. But if could you please refer to where in the report we have used this term, it might be useful. Well, I could add, I don't recall the OTP telling us to use that terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at P1776. This is the report from 2009, page 29 in the Serbian, last paragraph. Yes, that's right. Page 29 thus, and we can see that page. And it should be page 25 in English. Now we can see the document in both languages, as requested by the witness, and now I'm quoting a part of the report. This is the last paragraph in the Serbian, just below the figure: "Only a few young children (10 to 14 years of age) from the four municipalities went missing, but the proportions are very high for Srebrenica boys (31.8 per cent for ages 15 to 19 years) and young men (37.5 per cent for ages 20 to 24). In Srebrenica, the proportion of missing is extremely high for Muslim men of almost all ages: One third of all Muslim men between 15 and 17 went missing in 1995," and so on and so forth. I think that this is sufficient for you to recall that part of the report. My question is: Based on what do you call the age group from 15 to 19 boys?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Boys is not is a very precise term, but I think the age of maturity, legal maturity, is 18 in Bosnia, as in other countries. That means they are not of age yet, those who are below 18, then it is common to call them boys. We could have called them teenagers also. But I don't see the significance of this, whether they are called boys or young men or whatever, or teenagers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it have been then more favourable for you to set the age limit then at 18 instead of 19 years? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps so. But it is common in -- in demography to use five-year age groups starting with those ages beginning with 0 and 5, so 0 to 4, 5 to 9, 10 to 14, 15 to 19, et cetera, to reduce the number of numbers. And as you can see in Table 11 on the previous page, there are -- all the data are given by five-year age groups. But you're right, of course, age group 15 to 19 covers both, some who are definitely children, 15, and some who are young men, 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And does this also apply in the demographics of conflicts, this particular classification that you're using? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no standard age grouping in the demography of conflict. It is practical to use five-year age groups, sometimes ten-year age groups. If there's a special need or special goal of the analysis, then, of course, we can use other age groups. For example 15 to 17, if you want to focus on those who are not yet of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell us whether you investigated at what age men were engaged in Bosnia and Herzegovina into the military service and were there any among them who were younger than 16? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. I think OTP said something about that, that in some tables we were asked to see 16 and above, because soldiers could be as young in other cases, 18. I don't recall the exact age at what -- when young men joined the military or asked to do military service. And I guess perhaps it changed over the war period as well with the demands. Perhaps -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at 1D107 now, please. These are documents provided to the Prosecution, 135 killed and missing members of the B and H army. This is information that is provided to the OTP at their request. Now we're going look at that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 10 in the e-court. Page 10. Thank you. We can now see page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since there is no translation, I'm going to read it out: "At the request of the Defence administration of Tuzla and on the basis of Article 169 of the Law on Administrative Procedure, Official Gazette of Bosnia and Herzegovina, number 2/98, I issue the following certificate, confirming that Adil Porobic, son of Ramo, born on the 27th November, 1979, in Ljubovija, the municipality of Srebrenica, is entered into the records of the military unit as of the 17th of April, 1992, until the 12th of July, 1995. The above-named person, as a member of the B and H army, went missing on the 12th of July, 1995 on assignment." So that means that he went missing while he was on assignment". "The certificate is issued for the purposes of," so on and so forth, signed by Commander Colonel Dzevad Salibasic. Please, can you tell us how old this person was? All the required stamps are here on this document, as well as the ERN number given by the Prosecution. Can you please tell us how old this person was? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he was drafted he was 12 years and approximately five months, five, six months. And then on the 12th of July, 1995, he was 15 years and approximately eight months. He was young. I'm sad to see such young man having to fight in a war. Or young boys --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this certificate, as a document, testify to the fact that the military engaged on military assignments, even persons younger than 16? Here we have an example of a person aged 15 years and eight months. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think this person is not the right person to testify about the reliability of a document of another authority. You can draw your conclusions on that, I can do that, the Chamber can do that, everybody can do that. But it doesn't help you and your case if you ask a demographer who is here to testify about his expertise in demography. Please focus on the time you have used already during cross-examination. You should be aware of the need to have an expeditious, fair trial. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. But this is a certificate, and based on this certificate this person was registered in the missing persons list and similar other persons younger than 16. This witness worked on basis of this sort of data. Can we have now page 143. This is a certificate on a missing person, Nezir Mujcinovic, born on the 25th of October, 1979. He was registered as the member of the military on the 1st of February, 1993, and he went missing on the 12th of July, 1995, as a member of the ABiH performing an assignment on the way from Srebrenica to Tuzla. This has also been signed. So we can see that this person was only 13 years old when he was engaged by the ABiH and he was less than 16 when he took part in the breakthrough from Srebrenica to Tuzla, because here it actually says an assignment and their assignment was to break through.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is: Did you, as a demographer, research this peculiar phenomenon of engaging very, very young persons in the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, not. I would also object to the statement on line 2 of page 78 that this witness worked on the basis of this sort of data. Even if he had had such date, we wouldn't -- such certificates, we would not have used them. I don't see what we should have used them for. It's interesting but it's not part of our analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I said that the ICRC received information that those people went missing. I didn't say that you received it. It was the ICRC that put it into a list, that then, later on, you had to respect during your work. I wasn't pointing a finger at you. The only thing that I want to ask you now is as follows: According to your categorisation in your report, can we consider children younger than 16 to be members of the ABiH based on such certificates issued by the army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, obviously if these certificates are correct there were some young boys who were members of the army, whether all young boys, such young boys were members of the army or not we do not know. Whether these were unique, special cases or general, I don't know. And again, it doesn't make much difference -- it doesn't make any difference from our project which was to make a reliable list of missing or dead persons. We did not consider the military status of the -- of these -- well, I should add that we have compared a list of missing and dead persons with lists of soldiers from the ABiH, and we found that 70 per cent, approximately, of our missing and dead persons were on the ABiH list. So they were in -- in the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Dr. Brunborg, did you see such a certificate before like this one on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a clarification. Mr. Tolimir, you said at page 78, line 8, the witness worked on basis of this sort of data. This is, indeed, a misstatement, taking into account what the witness said. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would also like to add, Your Honour, he said that the ICRC based its work on such data, but they did not. They relied on statements from relatives of missing persons. I don't believe that -- I don't think they used such certificates at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I accept all criticisms of me, but I want you to answer the following question: Is it possible that this person was registered with the ICRC and included in their list of missing persons? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. 70 per cent of those registered as missing were soldiers, or at least were part of the army in some way or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have now P176 -- actually, 1776, which also dates from year 2009. Now we want to have page 26 in Serbian, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: While this is coming up, just for the record, the last document we have seen on the screen was not in your exhibit list we have received. Just to have that clear. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I thought it was, but, there you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here you say besides that many men aged 20 to 40 years probably took part in fighting and that's why they were elsewhere, or they were captured or killed and that's why they were not under the same risk of the -- of going missing from the enclave. Also: "It is probable that the youngest boys, aged 15 to 19, in 1995 were also less likely to be in the army, which may explain their elevated risk of disappearance compared to their preceding cohorts." My question is: Why did you determine the age group of men who probably took part in fighting as 20 to 40 years old and not 18 to 45 or to 60, because that was the end of the age of military conscription for -- for the military at the time? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. First I'd like to mention that yesterday I made it clear that there was -- there's a correction and that the last five words of that paragraph should be deleted. It was made clear yesterday, the second correction compared to the preceding cohorts. The reason here we talk about 20 to 40 years is that they had more uniform, we say, fatality rates. If you look at Table 11 which this refers to, you will see that when you come to age 45 or to 50 the fatality rates go up very much and we thought that this is speculation, that that would be used to several young -- the younger man being elsewhere, not being exposed to the risk. But, at the same time, there are many, 15 to 19, 20 to 24, who were indeed reported as missing. Some of them probably went to the forest. But remember here we compared -- we tried to get an estimate of the population at risk of being killed, if you like, or at least being reported as missing. And surprisingly this risk is highest for ages 45 to 54, more than 50 per cent. It is lower for the younger men. That is why -- what we tried to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Accepting everything you said, could you explain why do you deem it less probable that men aged 15 to 19 were in the army? I'm especially interested in this question bearing in mind the physical capabilities of men aged 15, 16, 17 to 19.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the simple reason that it is not common that people are drafted into the army at such young ages, at 15 or 16. Unfortunately, then in a war situation many are, indeed. But the certificates you showed to us are interesting, but they were only two examples and we don't know how frequently it is that such young men or boys, if you like, were drafted into the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You say they're only examples. But you have more similar certificates, the OTP has more similar certificates. I merely showed you two. Could you tell us whether you have a single case for which you can show documents when you talk about the combat activities of ABiH or is it what you just told us, your personal estimate? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't talk about combat activities of the ABiH. I was just trying to explain why -- why these fatality rates are so different, ranging from 31.8 for age group -- for Srebrenica men, 31.8 per cent, to 50.4 per cent for 45 to 49 ages. Perhaps I would like to ask you, but perhaps you're not allowed to answer. What was the minimum age for army soldiers in Bosnia before the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is not an appropriate question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- especially because we are over time now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We are just past 7.00. We have to adjourn for today. I am very sorry that you have to come back after the weekend. Mr. Tolimir, I would like to invite you to check your remaining questions. I don't think that it would be appropriate to have additional time. Six hours is really a lot, and you should try to comply with your own estimation and skip those questions which are repetitive and not really necessary to put to a demographer. We adjourn and resume Monday, I think in the morning at 9.00. I'm not sure about that. Monday, at 9.00, in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 14th of February, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.,
